issues: Re-fetched 2026-09-23. --check FOUND for the quote on the Cisco newsroom page, which is dated 'SAN JOSE, Calif., October 30, 2024'. The page footnote reads 'surveyed anonymously 2600 consumers in Australia, Brazil, China, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Spain, UK, US'. The full report PDF (cisco.com/c/dam/.../cisco-consumer-privacy-report-2024.pdf) says 'Respondents comprised 2600+ adults (18 years and older) in 12 countries', so '2,600+' and 12 countries are right. fetch-text.py gets HTTP 403 from cisco.com for the report; it was read through a WebFetch download and pdfminer, so it is not added as a --check source.

The report dates the fieldwork: 'As of June 2024, when our survey was conducted'. It confirms the 84% is among Gen AI users: 'Gen AI users seem to be highly aware ... 84% were concerned their data could be shared' (Figure 21, 'Data could be made public' 84%).

Caveat that belongs in the notes: the 30% headline is not in the report's text. The report's Figure 20 gives higher per-category shares of Gen AI users entering specific data: 'health information' 37%, 'work information' 36%, and '24% to 29%' for financial information, account numbers, religion/ethnicity, name and address. It is hard to reconcile these with only 30% entering 'personal or confidential information including financial and health details'. The value stands as Cisco's own published headline and is flagged, not changed.

fieldFixes.notes: 84% of Gen AI users in the same survey were concerned their data could be made public. Cisco's own consumer survey (double-blind online panel, fieldwork June 2024, 2,600+ adults in 12 countries); company research, not official statistics. The 30% is Cisco's press-release headline. The full report's category breakdown shows higher shares entering specific data types (health information 37%, work information 36%), so treat the figure as indicative.

issues: Re-fetched 2026-09-23. --check FOUND for the quote on the arXiv abstract page (v1 27 Oct 2023, v2 28 Jun 2024; comments '2024 ICLR Spotlight'). The PDF abstract words it slightly differently ('even commercial models such as GPT-4 and ChatGPT'), but the quote matches the abs page, which is the cited URL.

The label says 'Share of ConfAIde test cases', which misdescribes the population. The 57% is not a share of all benchmark cases. It is the Tier 4 result only, where the model acts as an AI meeting assistant, and the models were explicitly told to preserve privacy. The paper's introduction says: 'GPT-4 and ChatGPT reveal secrets 22% and 93% of the time in Tier 3, and flow information to inappropriate actors 39% and 57% of the time in Tier 4, even though they are directly instructed to preserve privacy.' Table 4 ('models are used as AI meeting assistants generating meeting summary and personal action items') gives ChatGPT 0.57 and GPT-4 0.39 on the 'Leaks Secret' row for the meeting-summary task. That is the average over 10 runs; the worst-case row is higher at 0.85 and 0.80. Table 5's 'w/o CoT' Tier 4 values (0.39 and 0.57) confirm this. The label, unit and notes are corrected.

The 'Leakage persisted with privacy-inducing prompts and chain-of-thought reasoning' note is supported by the abstract: 'This leakage persists even when we employ privacy-inducing prompts or chain-of-thought reasoning' (--check FOUND). The models are gpt-4-0613 and gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 (paper footnote).

fieldFixes.label: Share of ConfAIde Tier 4 meeting-assistant outputs in which ChatGPT leaked a secret to people who should not learn it, despite being told to preserve privacy
fieldFixes.unit: percent of outputs (Tier 4 meeting summaries, average over 10 runs)
fieldFixes.notes: GPT-4: 39%. In Tier 4 the model acts as an AI meeting assistant writing a meeting summary, and the figure is how often the summary discloses a secret discussed earlier in the meeting. The models were explicitly instructed to preserve privacy. The paper's abstract calls this revealing private information 'in contexts that humans would not'. In Tier 3 (short theory-of-mind scenarios) ChatGPT revealed secrets 93% of the time and GPT-4 22%. Leakage persisted with chain-of-thought prompting. Models tested: gpt-4-0613 and gpt-3.5-turbo-0613.

addSources.quote: GPT-4 and ChatGPT reveal secrets 22% and 93% of the time in Tier 3, and flow information to inappropriate actors 39% and 57% of the time in Tier 4, even though they are directly instructed to preserve privacy.
addSources.note: --check FOUND 2026-09-23 (v2 PDF). The same PDF has 'Table 4: Overview of metric values for Tier 4, where models are used as AI meeting assistants generating meeting summary and personal action items.' (--check FOUND) and 'This leakage is higher in the meeting summary task compared to the personal action item generation task.' (--check FOUND).

issues: Re-fetched 2026-09-23. --check FOUND for the quote on the arXiv abstract page (v1 29 Aug 2024; v3 14 Mar 2025; comments 'NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks Track'). Authors Shao, Li, Shi, Liu, Yang.

The label and notes say the 38.69% is the share of trajectories with a leak, but it is the paper's adjusted leakage rate (LRh), not the raw leakage rate. Table 2's caption: 'LR denotes the leakage rate; LRh denotes the adjusted leakage rate, considering only cases with positive helpfulness scores.' Under the Privacy-Enhancing Prompt, Table 2 gives Llama-3-70B-Instruct LR 39.15 and LRh 38.69, and GPT-4 LR 24.54 and LRh 25.68. The abstract's '25.68% and 38.69% of cases' are the LRh values. The headline is kept but the label, unit and notes now say what it measures, with the raw rates added. The model is Llama-3-70B-Instruct. There are 493 trajectories, and leakage was judged by a Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 classifier validated against human annotators.

fieldFixes.label: Share of PrivacyLens agent tasks in which Llama-3-70B leaked sensitive information despite privacy-enhancing instructions (helpfulness-adjusted rate)
fieldFixes.unit: percent of cases (adjusted leakage rate LRh: counted among agent final actions rated helpful)
fieldFixes.notes: GPT-4: 25.68%. These are the paper's adjusted leakage rates (LRh), counted only over agent final actions rated helpful. The unadjusted leakage rates with the same privacy-enhancing prompt are 39.15% for Llama-3-70B-Instruct and 24.54% for GPT-4. They are measured over 493 trajectories in which models act as agents carrying out user instructions (e.g. sending emails), not answering probing questions. Leakage was judged by a Mistral-7B classifier validated against human annotators.
